title: Adaptive batch strategy — throughput vs tail latency experiments
content:
TL;DR:
We ran a set of experiments to evaluate an adaptive batching release strategy that trades larger average throughput for predictable 99/99.9th percentile latency. The mechanism is a small age-penalty + entropy-based release that triggers when either batch reaches N_max or the oldest request age > T_age or an entropy threshold is hit (to prioritize short outputs).

Background / motivation:
- Current scheduler heuristics (size-or-time with fixed timeout) work okay for steady loads but produce wide tail variability under bursty/diurnal arrivals and mixed-RPC sizes.
- We want a small-footprint change to the scheduler to: 1) reduce 99.9% latency regressions, 2) preserve throughput for encoder-only/short-output workloads, and 3) remain compatible with existing autoscaling and caching plumbing.
- This doc captures: design, experiment matrix, workload generation, profiling notes, observed tradeoffs, and follow-ups.

Goals / success criteria:
- 99th and 99.9th latency reduce by at least 20% relative to baseline under bursty arrivals at 70% server capacity.
- Throughput drop < 7% (tokens/sec) for the same config on sustained high QPS for long-form generation workload.
- No increase in tail loss (dropped requests/timeouts) or CPU/GPU memory pressure spikes.

Hypotheses:
1) Introducing a small age-bias (requests accumulate "age score") will reduce head-of-line blocking for older requests and flatten tail latency without hurting average throughput much.
2) An entropy heuristic (based on predicted token distribution width from the first logits) can early-emit small batches that would otherwise wait, improving latency of short-output queries with negligible throughput cost.
3) Combining both heuristics with a conservative N_max cap yields best tail control with minimal throughput regression.

Experiment matrix (independent variables):
- N_max in {8, 16, 32} (model: Llama-2-13B quantized)
- T_timeout in {10ms, 20ms, 50ms} (batch release timeouts)
- Age penalty factor alpha in {0, 0.5, 1.0} (multiplies age into selection priority)
- Entropy threshold H_th in {none, 1.2, 2.0} (shannon bits from first-token logits estimate)
- Workloads: steady medium (70% cap), bursty (Poisson with bursts), mixed-size (short prompts vs long prompts 80/20).

Dependent metrics captured:
- p50/p90/p99/p99.9 request latency (end-to-end in serving runtime)
- tokens/sec and requests/sec
- GPU utilization, kernel queue lengths
- CPU scheduling stalls (threads waiting on queue lock)
- Batch size distribution over time (histogram)
- Number of preemptions / canceled batches
- Memory usage (host + GPU), peak allocs
- Percent of batches early-emitted due to entropy heuristic

Workload generation (how to reproduce):
- k6 + a small generator that reads prompt traces from prod-sampled-24h.json (sanitized). Bursty workload: Poisson lambda with superimposed 1s bursts at 5x baseline qps every 30s.
- Short prompt: mean response length 12 tokens. Long prompt: mean response length 400 tokens. Mixed ratio 80:20 for short:long.

Key scheduler changes (code pointers):
- Add age attribute to queued request struct; increment on wake/tick.
- Selection comparator: score = w_size * batch_size - alpha * age + w_entropy * (H_th - H_est) // pref emitting when H_est < H_th
- N_max is hard cap; timeouts still active. See PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/1789

Commands and profiling notes:
- Start experiment harness: ./tools/run_experiment --config experiments/adaptive-batch/exp-2024-10-02.yaml --prometheus 
- Collect pprof from runtime: curl localhost:6060/debug/pprof/profile?seconds=30 > profile.pb
- GPU traces: nsight systems for 30s windows around burst events; watch for kernel serialization and >90% SM occupancy drops (indicative of small-batch inefficiency)
- Flamegraph: go tool pprof -http=:8080 profile.pb (look at queue.lock and batcher.Wait)

Results (representative subset, bursty workload at 70% capacity):
Table layout (Config -> p50 / p99 / p99.9 / throughput):
- baseline (N_max=32, timeout=50ms, alpha=0, no entropy): p50=12ms, p99=180ms, p99.9=540ms, tput=100k tokens/s
- A (N_max=16, timeout=20ms, alpha=0.5, H_th=none): p50=13ms, p99=140ms, p99.9=300ms, tput=96k tokens/s
- B (N_max=16, timeout=20ms, alpha=0.5, H_th=1.2): p50=12ms, p99=125ms, p99.9=220ms, tput=95k tokens/s
- C (N_max=8, timeout=10ms, alpha=1.0, H_th=1.2): p50=16ms, p99=130ms, p99.9=210ms, tput=92k tokens/s

Observations / interpretation:
- Age penalty alpha>=0.5 consistently reduces 99.9th from ~500ms -> ~200-300ms on bursty traces. This matches Hypothesis 1.
- Entropy heuristic reduced latency of short prompts by 20-35% p99 (they stop getting stuck behind long generations). Percentage of batches early-emitted ~13% for H_th=1.2. Throughput impact small (~3-5%).
- Aggressive N_max=8 hurt p50 (because many early emissions create small-batch inefficiencies on GPU kernels) but still better tail. Tradeoff is clear: smaller N_max -> flatter tail, worse average token efficiency.
- Kernel profiling: small-batch inefficiency visible as SM underutilization when average batch size < 6. We should avoid pushing avg batch size below ~6 for Llama-2-13B on A100.
- CPU contention: the new comparator adds a tiny cost - spin profile shows queue.lock increases about 4% of CPU time under extreme bursts. Not a blocker.

Failure cases / caveats:
- In mixed workloads with a very high fraction of long-running requests (>40%), entropy heuristic sometimes misclassifies and emits small batches which serialize the GPU, hurting overall throughput by up to 12% in worst-case synthetic traces. Mitigation: only enable entropy for workloads with short-request ratio > 50% or adaptive gating based on observed batch-size histogram.
- Edge case: pods with very cold KV caches see longer per-request compute which amplifies the small-batch penalty. We need to gate N_max by an estimate of expected token-generation length (from model metadata or past requests).

Visualizations attached (TODO):
- batch_size_histogram.svg across time slices (burst windows)
- latency_percentile_plot.png (p50->p99.99) for configs A/B/C vs baseline
- flamegraphs: queue.lock vs batcher.Wait (before/after changes)

Actionable recommendations:
- Roll config B (N_max=16, timeout=20ms, alpha=0.5, H_th=1.2) to canary serving tier for 2 weeks behind a toggle. Expected: ~25-60% reduction in p99.9 on bursty traffic, ~5% throughput loss on sustained high throughput for mixed workloads.
- Add runtime metric: fraction_batches_early_emitted_by_entropy and avg_batch_size_by_model to the console. Create alert if avg_batch_size < 6 for Llama-2-13B family.
- Implement adaptive gating: entropy enabled only when short_request_ratio > 50% and avg_batch_size > 6.
- Follow-up experiments: try combining age-penalty with dynamic timeout (timeout = f(qps, age_histogram)) and evaluate end-to-end cost per token with Redwood Optimize suggestions.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Decide default N_max per model family (quantized vs fp16) and expose as model_config parameter? (TODO: RFC)
- Test on dedicated GPU types (T4 vs A100) to quantify small-batch inefficiency thresholds.
- Evaluate interaction with prefix caching: when prefix cache hit rates are high, early emits may produce duplicate computation; need to measure cache miss amplification.

Notes to self / rough logs:
- 2024-10-02: initial patch landed, saw immediate p99.9 drop in staging for dart-chatbot workload.
- 2024-10-09: added entropy thresholding after Sofia's offline analysis of first-logits variance.
- 2024-10-21: observed a weird regression under extremely long prompt mixes -> reverted entropy in that experiment, plan adaptive gating.

Links:
- Linear: RWI-412 (design and rollout plan)
- PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/1789
- Notes: confluence:serving-runtime/scheduler-design

If reviewers want, I can extract the raw experiment traces (+k6 scripts) to the artifacts bucket and attach configs. Next step: prepare canary rollout playbook and SLO guardrails (alert thresholds for avg_batch_size and tail-latency).

-- Aisha
